title: Merge k Sorted Lists
description: Brute force to optimized: sorting everything from scratch versus a min-heap-driven k-way merge that exploits each list already being sorted.

blocks.text: Given an array of k linked lists, each sorted in ascending order, merge all the lists into ONE sorted linked list and return its head.

blocks.caption: A min-heap always tracks the current smallest front node across all k lists, popping and replacing one at a time

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An array of k linked lists, each individually sorted in ascending order (any list may be empty)"],["Output","The head of a single linked list containing all values from every input list, fully sorted"],["Goal","Merge all k lists efficiently, ideally in O(N log k) time, where N is the total number of nodes across all lists"],["Constraints","0 <= k <= 10^4; 0 <= number of nodes in each list <= 500; -10^4 <= Node.val <= 10^4"]]}

blocks.text: Instead of merging just two sorted lists (a well-known simpler problem), this asks to merge k of them together into one fully sorted list, where k itself can be large.

blocks.title: Analogy: Merging k Sorted Stacks of Papers Into One
blocks.text: Imagine k separate stacks of numbered papers, each stack already sorted (smallest on top). To merge them all into one sorted stack, repeatedly look at the TOP paper of every stack, take whichever is smallest, and place it next. A min-heap makes "which stack currently has the smallest top paper" a fast lookup, rather than scanning all k stacks' tops every single time.

blocks.caption: Seed the heap with all k list heads; repeatedly pop the smallest and push its list's next node back in

blocks.text: Before sorting everything from scratch (ignoring that each list is ALREADY sorted), notice that a min-heap directly generalizes the classic two-list merge technique to any number of lists.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Merging just TWO sorted lists is simple: repeatedly compare their two current front nodes, take the smaller, advance that list.

Observation 2: With k lists, the same idea works, but comparing all k fronts one-by-one every single time would cost O(k) per output node, giving O(N*k) total.

Observation 3: A min-heap (priority queue) tracks the current smallest among UP TO k candidates in O(log k) per operation, rather than O(k), directly speeding up the repeated "which front is smallest" comparison.

Observation 4: Seeding the heap with each list's head, then repeatedly popping the smallest and pushing THAT SAME list's next node back in, correctly reproduces the merged order while never needing more than k items in the heap at once.

Recognizing this problem as "merge two sorted lists, but generalized to k using a heap for the repeated minimum-finding step" is the key pattern transfer.
This is a min-heap-driven k-way merge: exactly the two-list merge technique generalized using a priority queue to efficiently track the current smallest among k candidates.
Collect every value from every list into one big array, then sort that array directly, ignoring that each individual list was already sorted.

items: Walk through all k lists, appending every value into one combined array.
Sort the combined array using a standard comparison sort.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Collecting into a flat array first ignores each list's existing sorted order entirely, treating the problem as "sort N arbitrary numbers."
A standard library sort (typically O(N log N)) is used directly on the combined array.

blocks.text: Correctly produces a fully sorted combined result, since sorting works regardless of the input's original order.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(N log N), where N is the total number of nodes across all lists (a full sort ignoring the pre-existing per-list order).
Space: O(N), for the combined array.

Limitation: sorting from scratch wastes the fact that each list is ALREADY sorted; a min-heap-driven merge achieves O(N log k) instead, which is faster whenever k is smaller than N (the typical case).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force ignores that each list is pre-sorted, resorting everything from scratch at O(N log N). Instead, use a min-heap seeded with all k list heads. Repeatedly pop the current smallest node, append it to the result, and push that SAME list's next node back into the heap (if it exists). This never holds more than k nodes in the heap at once, giving O(N log k) total.

Seed a min-heap with each list's head node (skipping empty lists). Use a dummy head for the result. While the heap is non-empty: pop the smallest node, attach it to the result's tail, and if that node has a next, push it into the heap. Terminate the result's final tail with null.
Use a min-heap of size at most k to always know the current smallest front node across all lists, in O(log k) per operation.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The fully merged result is [1,1,2,3,4,4,5,6], matching the expected output.

codes.python:
import heapq

def merge_k_lists(lists):
    heap = []
    for i, node in enumerate(lists):
        if node:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.val, i, node))                       # (value, tie-breaker index, node) -- index avoids comparing nodes directly

    dummy = ListNode(0)
    tail = dummy
    while heap:
        val, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)                                  # always pop the CURRENT smallest front node across all lists
        tail.next = node
        tail = node
        if node.next:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))            # push that same list's next node back in
    tail.next = None
    return dummy.next


if __name__ == "__main__":
    lists = [
        ListNode(1, ListNode(4, ListNode(5))),
        ListNode(1, ListNode(3, ListNode(4))),
        ListNode(2, ListNode(6)),
    ]
    result = merge_k_lists(lists)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(N log k), where N is the total number of nodes and k is the number of lists: each of the N nodes is pushed and popped exactly once, each operation costing O(log k).
Space: O(k), the heap never holds more than one node per list at a time.

At every point, the heap contains exactly one "candidate" node per non-exhausted list: specifically, the earliest not-yet-output node of that list. Since each list is individually sorted, that candidate is always the SMALLEST remaining value from its own list. The heap's pop operation correctly picks the smallest among all these candidates, guaranteeing the overall output is fully sorted, one node at a time.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A list is empty from the start","Simply never seeded into the heap, contributing nothing"],["A list becomes exhausted (its current node has no next)","Nothing is pushed back for it; the heap naturally shrinks"],["Heap becomes empty","All lists are exhausted; the merge is complete"]]}

items: The heap must be seeded with EVERY list's head (skipping null/empty lists), establishing one initial candidate per list.
A tie-breaking index (in the Python version) avoids comparing ListNode objects directly when two values are equal, since nodes are not inherently comparable.
The result is built with a dummy head, exactly like the two-list merge technique, avoiding special-casing the very first node.

blocks.text: Merging k already-sorted sequences generalizes the classic two-way merge using a min-heap, which efficiently tracks the current smallest among k candidates in O(log k) per step, rather than scanning all k every time.

items: Comparing ListNode objects directly in languages/heaps that need a well-defined ordering, without a tie-breaker for equal values (can cause runtime errors in some heap implementations).
Forgetting to push a popped node's NEXT node back into the heap, which would silently drop the rest of that list.
Not skipping null/empty lists when seeding the initial heap, which could crash on a null dereference.

items: Explicitly starting from "how would you merge just 2 sorted lists?" and then generalizing to k using a heap demonstrates the exact reasoning path this problem is designed to test.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Merge K sorted [lists/arrays/streams]" points directly toward a min-heap holding one current candidate per source, generalizing the standard two-way merge.

items: How else could this be solved without a heap? A divide-and-conquer approach (pairwise merging the k lists, similar to merge sort's combine step) also achieves O(N log k) time.

What is the space complexity difference between the heap approach and divide-and-conquer? The heap approach uses O(k) extra space; divide-and-conquer additionally needs O(log k) recursion stack depth.
How would this scale if k were extremely large (say, 10^6) but each list very short? The O(log k) heap factor grows slowly, so this approach remains efficient even as k scales up.
A direct k-way generalization of the two-list merge technique used in Merge Two Sorted Lists and internally within Sort List's merge sort, elsewhere in this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(N log N) time, O(N) space.
Optimized (min-heap k-way merge): O(N log k) time, O(k) space.

items: Pattern: Min-heap-driven k-way merge
Core Idea: Seed a min-heap with each list's head; repeatedly pop the current smallest and push that same list's next node back in, generalizing the two-list merge to k lists
Time: O(N log k)
Space: O(k)
Most Important Observation: The heap only ever needs to hold ONE candidate per list at a time (the earliest not-yet-output node), since each list is individually pre-sorted
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Seed heap with k heads; pop smallest, push its next, repeat until empty
